claim: Bacterial and eukaryotic nuclear RNA polymerases (RNAPs) cap RNA with NAD+ and NADH using NAD+ and NADH as non-canonical initiating nucleotides for transcription initiation.
source: Bacterial and eukaryotic nuclear RNA polymerases (RNAPs) cap RNA with the oxidized and reduced forms of the metabolic effector nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, NAD+ and NADH, using NAD+ and NADH as non-canonical initiating nucleotides for transcription initiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work establishing NCIN-mediated capping in bacterial and nuclear RNAPs.

claim: Mitochondrial RNAPs (mtRNAPs) cap RNA with NAD+ and NADH.
source: Here, we show that mitochondrial RNAPs (mtRNAPs) cap RNA with NAD+ and NADH, and do so more efficiently than nuclear RNAPs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2 demonstrating NCIN-mediated capping by mtRNAPs.

claim: Mitochondrial RNAPs cap RNA with NAD+ and NADH more efficiently than nuclear RNAPs.
source: Here, we show that mitochondrial RNAPs (mtRNAPs) cap RNA with NAD+ and NADH, and do so more efficiently than nuclear RNAPs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2 comparing capping efficiencies between mtRNAPs and nuclear RNAPs.

claim: Up to ~60% of yeast mitochondrial transcripts are capped with NAD+ and NADH in vivo.
source: Direct quantitation of NAD+- and NADH-capped RNA demonstrates remarkably high levels of capping in vivo: up to ~60% NAD+ and NADH capping of yeast mitochondrial transcripts, and up to ~15% NAD+ capping of human mitochondrial transcripts.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from boronate affinity electrophoresis experiments shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Up to ~15% of human mitochondrial transcripts are capped with NAD+ in vivo.
source: Direct quantitation of NAD+- and NADH-capped RNA demonstrates remarkably high levels of capping in vivo: up to ~60% NAD+ and NADH capping of yeast mitochondrial transcripts, and up to ~15% NAD+ capping of human mitochondrial transcripts.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from boronate affinity electrophoresis experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Capping efficiency is determined by promoter sequence at, and upstream of, the transcription start site.
source: The capping efficiency is determined by promoter sequence at, and upstream of, the transcription start site and, in yeast and human cells, by intracellular NAD+ and NADH levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 3 showing effects of promoter sequence variations on capping efficiency.

claim: In yeast and human cells, capping efficiency is determined by intracellular NAD+ and NADH levels.
source: The capping efficiency is determined by promoter sequence at, and upstream of, the transcription start site and, in yeast and human cells, by intracellular NAD+ and NADH levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 5 showing changes in capping levels under different metabolic conditions.

claim: mtRNAPs serve as both sensors and actuators in coupling cellular metabolism to mitochondrial transcriptional outputs.
source: Our findings indicate mtRNAPs serve as both sensors and actuators in coupling cellular metabolism to mitochondrial transcriptional outputs, sensing NAD+ and NADH levels and adjusting transcriptional outputs accordingly.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing correlation between NAD+/NADH levels and capping patterns.

claim: mtRNAPs sense NAD+ and NADH levels and adjust transcriptional outputs accordingly.
source: Our findings indicate mtRNAPs serve as both sensors and actuators in coupling cellular metabolism to mitochondrial transcriptional outputs, sensing NAD+ and NADH levels and adjusting transcriptional outputs accordingly.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data in Figure 5 showing changes in capping patterns correlate with metabolic conditions.

claim: An m7G cap is added to many eukaryotic messenger RNAs.
source: One well-characterized RNA 5'-end modification is the 'cap' comprising 7-methylguanylate (m7G) added to many eukaryotic messenger RNAs (Furuichi and Shatkin, 2000; Shatkin, 1976; Shuman, 1995; Wei et al., 1975).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on m7G capping.

claim: A new RNA 5'-end cap comprising NAD has been shown to be added to certain RNAs isolated from bacterial, yeast, and human cells.
source: Recently, a new RNA 5'-end cap comprising the metabolic effector nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) has been shown to be added to certain RNAs isolated from bacterial, yeast, and human cells (Cahová et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2009; Frindert et al., 2018; Jiao et al., 2017; Walters et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work identifying NAD-capped RNAs in various organisms.

claim: An m7G cap is added to nascent RNA by a capping complex that associates with eukaryotic RNA polymerase II.
source: In contrast to a m7G cap, which is added to nascent RNA by a capping complex that associates with eukaryotic RNA polymerase II (RNAP II) (Ghosh and Lima, 2010; Martinez-Rucobo et al., 2015; Shuman, 1995; Shuman, 2001; Shuman, 2015), an NAD cap is added by RNAP itself during transcription initiation, by serving as a non-canonical initiating nucleotide (NCIN) (Bird et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on m7G capping mechanisms.

claim: An NAD cap is added by RNAP itself during transcription initiation, by serving as a non-canonical initiating nucleotide (NCIN).
source: In contrast to a m7G cap, which is added to nascent RNA by a capping complex that associates with eukaryotic RNA polymerase II (RNAP II) (Ghosh and Lima, 2010; Martinez-Rucobo et al., 2015; Shuman, 1995; Shuman, 2001; Shuman, 2015), an NAD cap is added by RNAP itself during transcription initiation, by serving as a non-canonical initiating nucleotide (NCIN) (Bird et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work demonstrating NCIN-mediated NAD capping.

claim: NCIN-mediated NAD capping has been demonstrated for bacterial RNAP.
source: NCIN-mediated NAD capping has been demonstrated for bacterial RNAP (Bird et al., 2016; Frindert et al., 2018; Julius and Yuzenkova, 2017; Vvedenskaya et al., 2018) and eukaryotic RNAP II (Bird et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on bacterial RNAP.

claim: NCIN-mediated NAD capping has been demonstrated for eukaryotic RNAP II.
source: NCIN-mediated NAD capping has been demonstrated for bacterial RNAP (Bird et al., 2016; Frindert et al., 2018; Julius and Yuzenkova, 2017; Vvedenskaya et al., 2018) and eukaryotic RNAP II (Bird et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on eukaryotic RNAP II.

claim: m7G capping occurs after transcription initiation, on formation of the ~20th phosphodiester bond.
source: Thus, whereas m7G capping occurs after transcription initiation, on formation of the ~20th phosphodiester bond, and occurs only in organisms harboring specialized capping complexes, NAD capping occurs in transcription initiation, on formation of the first phosphodiester bond, and because it is performed by RNAP itself, is likely to occur in most, if not all, organisms.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of m7G capping mechanisms.

claim: m7G capping occurs only in organisms harboring specialized capping complexes.
source: Thus, whereas m7G capping occurs after transcription initiation, on formation of the ~20th phosphodiester bond, and occurs only in organisms harboring specialized capping complexes, NAD capping occurs in transcription initiation, on formation of the first phosphodiester bond, and because it is performed by RNAP itself, is likely to occur in most, if not all, organisms.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of m7G capping mechanisms.

claim: NAD capping occurs in transcription initiation, on formation of the first phosphodiester bond.
source: Thus, whereas m7G capping occurs after transcription initiation, on formation of the ~20th phosphodiester bond, and occurs only in organisms harboring specialized capping complexes, NAD capping occurs in transcription initiation, on formation of the first phosphodiester bond, and because it is performed by RNAP itself, is likely to occur in most, if not all, organisms.
evidence: This claim is based on prior work demonstrating NCIN-mediated capping mechanism.

claim: NAD capping is likely to occur in most, if not all, organisms because it is performed by RNAP itself.
source: Thus, whereas m7G capping occurs after transcription initiation, on formation of the ~20th phosphodiester bond, and occurs only in organisms harboring specialized capping complexes, NAD capping occurs in transcription initiation, on formation of the first phosphodiester bond, and because it is performed by RNAP itself, is likely to occur in most, if not all, organisms.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the mechanism of NAD capping.

claim: NAD exists in oxidized and reduced forms: NAD+ and NADH, respectively.
source: NAD exists in oxidized and reduced forms: NAD+ and NADH, respectively (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is based on established biochemical knowledge and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Capping with NAD+ has been demonstrated both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Capping with NAD+ has been demonstrated both in vitro and in vivo (Bird et al., 2016; Frindert et al., 2018; Julius and Yuzenkova, 2017; Vvedenskaya et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work demonstrating NAD+ capping.

claim: Capping with NADH has been demonstrated in vitro.
source: Capping with NADH has been demonstrated in vitro (Bird et al., 2016; Julius and Yuzenkova, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work demonstrating NADH capping in vitro.

claim: The identified Saccharomyces cerevisiae NAD+-capped RNAs included RNAs produced by mitochondrial RNAP.
source: Notably, the identified Saccharomyces cerevisiae NAD+-capped RNAs included not only RNAs produced by nuclear RNAPs, but also RNAs produced by mitochondrial RNAP (mtRNAP).
evidence: This claim is based on prior work by Parker, Kiledjian, and co-workers using NAD captureSeq.

claim: Eukaryotic nuclear RNAPs are multi-subunit RNAPs closely related in sequence and structure to bacterial RNAP.
source: The eukaryotic nuclear RNAPs--RNAP I, II, and III--are multi-subunit RNAPs closely related in sequence and structure to bacterial RNAP (Cramer, 2002; Darst, 2001; Ebright, 2000; Werner and Grohmann, 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on RNAP structure and evolution.

claim: mtRNAPs are single-subunit RNAPs that are unrelated in sequence and structure to multi-subunit RNAPs.
source: in contrast, mtRNAPs are single-subunit RNAPs that are unrelated in sequence and structure to multi-subunit RNAPs and, instead, are related to DNA polymerases, reverse transcriptases, and DNA-dependent RNAPs from T7-like bacteriophages (Cermakian et al., 1996; Cheetham and Steitz, 2000; Hillen et al., 2018; Masters et al., 1987; McAllister and Raskin, 1993; Ringel et al., 2011; Sousa, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on mtRNAP structure and evolution.

claim: mtRNAPs are related to DNA polymerases, reverse transcriptases, and DNA-dependent RNAPs from T7-like bacteriophages.
source: in contrast, mtRNAPs are single-subunit RNAPs that are unrelated in sequence and structure to multi-subunit RNAPs and, instead, are related to DNA polymerases, reverse transcriptases, and DNA-dependent RNAPs from T7-like bacteriophages (Cermakian et al., 1996; Cheetham and Steitz, 2000; Hillen et al., 2018; Masters et al., 1987; McAllister and Raskin, 1993; Ringel et al., 2011; Sousa, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on mtRNAP evolutionary relationships.

claim: S. cerevisiae mtRNAP generates initial RNA products using NAD+ and NADH as NCINs.
source: The results establish that S. cerevisiae mtRNAP and human mtRNAP are able to generate initial RNA products using NAD+ and NADH as NCINs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C demonstrating initial product formation.

claim: Human mtRNAP generates initial RNA products using NAD+ and NADH as NCINs.
source: The results establish that S. cerevisiae mtRNAP and human mtRNAP are able to generate initial RNA products using NAD+ and NADH as NCINs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D demonstrating initial product formation.

claim: S. cerevisiae mtRNAP generates full-length RNA products using NAD+ and NADH as NCINs.
source: The results establish that S. cerevisiae mtRNAP and human mtRNAP not only generate initial RNA products, but also generate full-length RNA products, using NAD+ and NADH as NCINs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C (bottom) demonstrating full-length product formation.

claim: Human mtRNAP generates full-length RNA products using NAD+ and NADH as NCINs.
source: The results establish that S. cerevisiae mtRNAP and human mtRNAP not only generate initial RNA products, but also generate full-length RNA products, using NAD+ and NADH as NCINs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D (bottom) demonstrating full-length product formation.

claim: The relative efficiency (kcat/KM)NCIN / (kcat/KM)ATP for NCIN-mediated initiation with NAD+ by S. cerevisiae mtRNAP is ~0.3 to ~0.4.
source: We obtained values of (kcat/KM)NCIN / (kcat/KM)ATP of ~0.3 to ~0.4 for NCIN-mediated initiation with NAD+ and NADH by S. cerevisiae mtRNAP and ~0.2 to ~0.6 for NCIN-mediated initiation with NAD+ and NADH by human mtRNAP.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from in vitro transcription assays shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The relative efficiency (kcat/KM)NCIN / (kcat/KM)ATP for NCIN-mediated initiation with NADH by S. cerevisiae mtRNAP is ~0.3 to ~0.4.
source: We obtained values of (kcat/KM)NCIN / (kcat/KM)ATP of ~0.3 to ~0.4 for NCIN-mediated initiation with NAD+ and NADH by S. cerevisiae mtRNAP and ~0.2 to ~0.6 for NCIN-mediated initiation with NAD+ and NADH by human mtRNAP.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from in vitro transcription assays shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The relative efficiency (kcat/KM)NCIN / (kcat/KM)ATP for NCIN-mediated initiation with NAD+ by human mtRNAP is ~0.2 to ~0.6.
source: We obtained values of (kcat/KM)NCIN / (kcat/KM)ATP of ~0.3 to ~0.4 for NCIN-mediated initiation with NAD+ and NADH by S. cerevisiae mtRNAP and ~0.2 to ~0.6 for NCIN-mediated initiation with NAD+ and NADH by human mtRNAP.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from in vitro transcription assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The relative efficiency (kcat/KM)NCIN / (kcat/KM)ATP for NCIN-mediated initiation with NADH by human mtRNAP is ~0.2 to ~0.6.
source: We obtained values of (kcat/KM)NCIN / (kcat/KM)ATP of ~0.3 to ~0.4 for NCIN-mediated initiation with NAD+ and NADH by S. cerevisiae mtRNAP and ~0.2 to ~0.6 for NCIN-mediated initiation with NAD+ and NADH by human mtRNAP.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from in vitro transcription assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: NCIN-mediated initiation with NAD+ or NADH is up to 40% as efficient as initiation with ATP for S. cerevisiae mtRNAP.
source: These values imply that NCIN-mediated initiation with NAD+ or NADH is up to 40% as efficient as initiation with ATP for S. cerevisiae mtRNAP and up to 60% as efficient as initiation with ATP for human mtRNAP.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the measured relative efficiency values.

claim: NCIN-mediated initiation with NAD+ or NADH is up to 60% as efficient as initiation with ATP for human mtRNAP.
source: These values imply that NCIN-mediated initiation with NAD+ or NADH is up to 40% as efficient as initiation with ATP for S. cerevisiae mtRNAP and up to 60% as efficient as initiation with ATP for human mtRNAP.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the measured relative efficiency values.

claim: The observed efficiencies of NCIN-mediated initiation with NAD+ or NADH by mtRNAPs are substantially higher than the highest previously reported efficiencies for NCIN-mediated initiation with NAD+ or NADH by cellular RNAPs (~15%).
source: The observed efficiencies of NCIN-mediated initiation with NAD+ or NADH by mtRNAPs are substantially higher than the highest previously reported efficiencies for NCIN-mediated initiation with NAD+ or NADH by cellular RNAPs (~15%; Bird et al., 2017; Bird et al., 2016; Vvedenskaya et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of current data to prior work cited.

claim: Efficiencies of NCIN-mediated initiation with NAD+ and NADH by mtRNAP are ~10 to ~40 fold higher than efficiencies of NCIN-mediated initiation with NAD+ and NADH by E. coli RNAP and S. cerevisiae RNAP II.
source: In these experiments, we observe efficiencies of NCIN-mediated initiation with NAD+ and NADH by mtRNAP that are fully ~10 to ~40 fold higher than efficiencies of NCIN-mediated initiation with NAD+ and NADH by E. coli RNAP and S. cerevisiae RNAP II (Figure 2C, bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C comparing different RNAPs.

claim: S. cerevisiae mtRNAP and human mtRNAP cap RNA with NAD+ and NADH more efficiently than bacterial RNAP and eukaryotic nuclear RNAP II.
source: We conclude that S. cerevisiae mtRNAP and human mtRNAP cap RNA with NAD+ and NADH more efficiently than bacterial RNAP and eukaryotic nuclear RNAP II.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2C comparing capping efficiencies.

claim: The efficiencies of NCIN-mediated initiation with NAD+ and NADH by T7 RNAP are nearly as high as the efficiencies of NCIN-mediated initiation by mtRNAPs.
source: The efficiencies of NCIN-mediated initiation with NAD+ and NADH by T7 RNAP were nearly as high as the efficiencies of NCIN-mediated initiation by mtRNAPs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is a quantitative difference in the efficiency of NCIN capping between members of the single-subunit RNAP family (T7 RNAP and mtRNAPs) and members of the multi-subunit RNAP family (bacterial RNAP and eukaryotic nuclear RNAP II).
source: We conclude that there is a quantitative difference in the efficiency of NCIN capping between members of the single-subunit RNAP family (T7 RNAP and mtRNAPs) and members of the multi-subunit RNAP family (bacterial RNAP and eukaryotic nuclear RNAP II).
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparison of capping efficiencies across different RNAP families.

claim: NCIN capping by bacterial RNAP is determined by promoter sequence, particularly at and immediately upstream of, the transcription start site.
source: In previous work, we have shown that NCIN capping with NAD+ and NADH by bacterial RNAP is determined by promoter sequence, particularly at and immediately upstream of, the transcription start site (TSS) (Bird et al., 2016; Vvedenskaya et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on bacterial RNAP.

claim: NCIN capping by bacterial RNAP occurs only at promoters where the base pair at the TSS is A:T (+1A promoters).
source: NCIN capping by bacterial RNAP occurs only at promoters where the base pair (nontemplate-strand base:template-strand base) at the TSS is A:T (+1A promoters), and occurs most efficiently at the subset of +1A promoters where the base pair immediately upstream of the TSS is purine:pyrimidine (−1R promoters).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on bacterial RNAP.

claim: NCIN capping by bacterial RNAP occurs most efficiently at the subset of +1A promoters where the base pair immediately upstream of the TSS is purine:pyrimidine (−1R promoters).
source: NCIN capping by bacterial RNAP occurs only at promoters where the base pair (nontemplate-strand base:template-strand base) at the TSS is A:T (+1A promoters), and occurs most efficiently at the subset of +1A promoters where the base pair immediately upstream of the TSS is purine:pyrimidine (−1R promoters).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on bacterial RNAP.

claim: Sequence determinants for NCIN capping by bacterial RNAP reside within the template strand of promoter DNA.
source: We have further shown that sequence determinants for NCIN capping by bacterial RNAP reside within the template strand of promoter DNA (i.e., the strand that templates incoming nucleotide substrates) (Vvedenskaya et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on bacterial RNAP.

claim: NAD+ capping by S. cerevisiae mtRNAP occurs only with promoter derivatives having A:T at position +1.
source: We observed NAD+ capping in reactions performed using the promoter derivative having A:T at position +1, but not in reactions performed using the promoter derivative having G:C at position +1 (Figure 3B), indicating specificity for A:T at position +1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Specificity at position +1 for NAD+ capping by S. cerevisiae mtRNAP resides in the template strand.
source: We observed NAD+ capping only with the promoter derivative having T as the template strand base at position +1, indicating that specificity at position +1 resides in the template strand.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B using heteroduplex templates.

claim: Higher efficiencies of NAD+ capping are observed with promoter derivatives having R:Y at position −1 than with promoter derivatives having Y:R.
source: We observed higher efficiencies of NAD+ capping with promoter derivatives having R:Y at position −1 than with promoter derivatives having Y:R (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Sequence information for NAD+ capping with S. cerevisiae mtRNAP resides exclusively in the template strand.
source: Furthermore, within error, the capping efficiencies for promoter derivatives having Y or R at template-strand position −1 matched the capping efficiencies for homoduplex promoter derivatives (Figure 3C–D), indicating that sequence information for NAD+ capping with S. cerevisiae mtRNAP resides exclusively in the template strand.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3C-D comparing homoduplex and heteroduplex templates.

claim: NCIN capping with NAD+ by mtRNAP is determined by the sequence at, and immediately upstream of, the TSS (positions +1 and −1, respectively).
source: We conclude that NCIN capping with NAD+ by mtRNAP is determined by the sequence at, and immediately upstream of, the TSS (positions +1 and −1, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 3 showing effects of sequence variations at positions +1 and -1.

claim: The sequence and strand preferences at positions +1 and −1 for NCIN capping with NAD+ by mtRNAP match the sequence and strand preferences observed for bacterial RNAP.
source: We further conclude that the sequence and strand preferences at positions +1 and −1 for NCIN capping with NAD+ by mtRNAP match the sequence and strand preferences observed for bacterial RNAP (Figure 3C–E) (Bird et al., 2016; Vvedenskaya et al., 2018), suggesting that these sequence and strand preferences may be universal determinants of NCIN capping with NAD+ for all RNAPs.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of data in Figure 3 to prior work on bacterial RNAP.

claim: Sequence and strand preferences at positions +1 and −1 may be universal determinants of NCIN capping with NAD+ for all RNAPs.
source: We further conclude that the sequence and strand preferences at positions +1 and −1 for NCIN capping with NAD+ by mtRNAP match the sequence and strand preferences observed for bacterial RNAP (Figure 3C–E) (Bird et al., 2016; Vvedenskaya et al., 2018), suggesting that these sequence and strand preferences may be universal determinants of NCIN capping with NAD+ for all RNAPs.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from observed similarities across different RNAPs.

claim: Sequence preferences for NCIN capping with NAD+ by bacteriophage T7 RNAP match the sequence preferences observed for S. cerevisiae mtRNAP and bacterial RNAP.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we find that sequence preferences for NCIN capping with NAD+ by bacteriophage T7 RNAP, another member of the single-subunit RNAP family, match the sequence preferences observed for S. cerevisiae mtRNAP and bacterial RNAP (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The basis for sequence and strand preferences for NCIN capping is a strict requirement for template-strand +1T for base pairing to the NAD+ adenine moiety.
source: Further consistent with this hypothesis, structural modeling suggests the basis for these sequence and strand preferences is universal: specifically, a strict requirement for template-strand +1T for base pairing to the NAD+ adenine moiety, and a preference for template strand −1Y for 'pseudo' base pairing to the NAD+ nicotinamide moiety (Bird et al., 2016; Vvedenskaya et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is based on structural modeling and inference from prior work.

claim: The basis for sequence and strand preferences for NCIN capping is a preference for template strand −1Y for 'pseudo' base pairing to the NAD+ nicotinamide moiety.
source: Further consistent with this hypothesis, structural modeling suggests the basis for these sequence and strand preferences is universal: specifically, a strict requirement for template-strand +1T for base pairing to the NAD+ adenine moiety, and a preference for template strand −1Y for 'pseudo' base pairing to the NAD+ nicotinamide moiety (Bird et al., 2016; Vvedenskaya et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is based on structural modeling and inference from prior work.

claim: Boronate affinity electrophoresis allows resolution of uncapped RNAs from capped RNAs that contain a vicinal-diol moiety.
source: Kössel, Jäschke and co-workers have demonstrated that boronate affinity electrophoresis allows resolution of uncapped RNAs from capped RNAs--such as m7G, NAD+ and NADH--that contain a vicinal-diol moiety (Igloi and Kössel, 1985; Igloi and Kössel, 1987; Nübel et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on boronate affinity electrophoresis.

claim: Boronate affinity electrophoresis does not allow resolution of RNAs longer than ~200 nt.
source: However, the procedures of Kössel, Jäschke and co-workers have two limitations: (i) boronate affinity electrophoresis does not allow resolution of RNAs longer than ~200 nt, and (ii) boronate affinity electrophoresis, by itself, is unable to distinguish between different vicinal-diol containing cap structures (m7G, NAD+, NADH, or others).
evidence: This claim is based on known limitations of the boronate affinity electrophoresis method.

claim: Boronate affinity electrophoresis, by itself, is unable to distinguish between different vicinal-diol containing cap structures (m7G, NAD+, NADH, or others).
source: However, the procedures of Kössel, Jäschke and co-workers have two limitations: (i) boronate affinity electrophoresis does not allow resolution of RNAs longer than ~200 nt, and (ii) boronate affinity electrophoresis, by itself, is unable to distinguish between different vicinal-diol containing cap structures (m7G, NAD+, NADH, or others).
evidence: This claim is based on known limitations of the boronate affinity electrophoresis method.

claim: S. cerevisiae mitochondrial RNAs COX2 and 21S were previously detected as NAD+-capped.
source: We selected for analysis two S. cerevisiae mitochondrial RNAs that previously had been detected as NAD+-capped: COX2 and 21S (Walters et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Walters et al.

claim: Both COX2 and 21S RNAs are present in NAD+-capped forms in S. cerevisiae.
source: The results show that both COX2 and 21S RNAs are present in NAD+-capped forms, and that COX2 RNA also is present in an NADH-capped-form.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4C-D and 5A.

claim: COX2 RNA is present in an NADH-capped form in S. cerevisiae.
source: The results show that both COX2 and 21S RNAs are present in NAD+-capped forms, and that COX2 RNA also is present in an NADH-capped-form.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4C-D and 5A.

claim: S. cerevisiae mitochondrial RNAs undergo NAD+ capping at 5' ends generated by transcription initiation.
source: The results confirm that S. cerevisiae mitochondrial RNAs undergo NAD+ capping in cells, show that S. cerevisiae mitochondrial RNAs undergo NAD+ capping at 5' ends generated by transcription initiation (as opposed to 5' ends generated by RNA processing), and show that S. cerevisiae mitochondrial RNAs also undergo NADH capping in cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using DNAzyme cleavage and boronate affinity electrophoresis.

claim: S. cerevisiae mitochondrial RNAs undergo NADH capping in cells.
source: The results confirm that S. cerevisiae mitochondrial RNAs undergo NAD+ capping in cells, show that S. cerevisiae mitochondrial RNAs undergo NAD+ capping at 5' ends generated by transcription initiation (as opposed to 5' ends generated by RNA processing), and show that S. cerevisiae mitochondrial RNAs also undergo NADH capping in cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: For COX2 RNA, NAD+-capped RNA comprises ~50% of the total COX2 RNA pool.
source: For COX2 RNA, NAD+-capped RNA comprises ~50% of the total COX2 RNA pool and NADH-capped RNA comprises ~10% of the total COX2 RNA pool (Figures 4C–D and 5A, top).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from boronate affinity electrophoresis shown in Figures 4C-D and 5A.

claim: For COX2 RNA, NADH-capped RNA comprises ~10% of the total COX2 RNA pool.
source: For COX2 RNA, NAD+-capped RNA comprises ~50% of the total COX2 RNA pool and NADH-capped RNA comprises ~10% of the total COX2 RNA pool (Figures 4C–D and 5A, top).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from boronate affinity electrophoresis shown in Figures 4C-D and 5A.

claim: For 21S RNA, NAD+-capped RNA comprises ~30% of the total 21S RNA pool.
source: For 21S RNA, NAD+-capped RNA comprises ~30% of the total 21S RNA pool (Figure 5A, top).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from boronate affinity electrophoresis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: These levels of NCIN capping are ~2 to ~50 times higher than levels of NCIN-capping in exponentially growing E. coli.
source: These levels of NCIN capping are ~2 to ~50 times higher than levels of NCIN-capping in exponentially growing E. coli (less than 1% to ~20% for NAD+-capping; not previously detected for NADH-capping) (Bird et al., 2016; Cahová et al., 2015; Nübel et al., 2017; Vvedenskaya et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of current data to prior work on E. coli.

claim: Human mitochondrial RNAs undergo NAD+ capping in cells.
source: The results establish that human mitochondrial RNAs undergo NAD+ capping in cells and show that human mitochondrial RNAs undergo NAD+ capping at 5' ends generated by transcription initiation (as opposed to 5' ends generated by RNA processing).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Human mitochondrial RNAs undergo NAD+ capping at 5' ends generated by transcription initiation.
source: The results establish that human mitochondrial RNAs undergo NAD+ capping in cells and show that human mitochondrial RNAs undergo NAD+ capping at 5' ends generated by transcription initiation (as opposed to 5' ends generated by RNA processing).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using DNAzyme cleavage and boronate affinity electrophoresis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Mitochondria are the primary locus of metabolism and energy transformation in the eukaryotic cell.
source: Mitochondria are the primary locus of metabolism and energy transformation in the eukaryotic cell, serving as the venue for the tricarboxylic acid cycle (TCA) cycle and oxidative phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of mitochondrial function.

claim: Mitochondria serve as the venue for the tricarboxylic acid cycle (TCA) cycle and oxidative phosphorylation.
source: Mitochondria are the primary locus of metabolism and energy transformation in the eukaryotic cell, serving as the venue for the tricarboxylic acid cycle (TCA) cycle and oxidative phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of mitochondrial function.

claim: The TCA cycle reduces NAD+ to NADH.
source: The TCA cycle reduces NAD+ to NADH and oxidative phosphorylation oxidizes NADH to NAD+.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of metabolic pathways.

claim: Oxidative phosphorylation oxidizes NADH to NAD+.
source: The TCA cycle reduces NAD+ to NADH and oxidative phosphorylation oxidizes NADH to NAD+.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of metabolic pathways.

claim: mtRNAPs perform NCIN capping with NAD+ and NADH at efficiencies that vary in a simple mass-action-dependent fashion with [NAD+] / [ATP] and [NADH] / [ATP] ratios in vitro.
source: Our finding that mtRNAPs perform NCIN capping with NAD+ and NADH at efficiencies that vary in a simple mass-action-dependent fashion with [NAD+] / [ATP] and [NADH] / [ATP] ratios in vitro (Figures 1 and 2), and our finding that mtRNAPs perform efficient NCIN capping to yield NAD+- and NADH-capped mitochondrial RNAs in vivo (Figures 4 and 5), raise the possibility that mtRNAPs may serve as both sensors and actuators in coupling metabolism to mitochondrial gene expression in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Changing from a growth condition yielding a high [NAD+] / [NADH] ratio to a growth condition yielding a low [NAD+] / [NADH] ratio results in a decrease in levels of NAD+ capping of COX2 RNA (from ~50% to ~20%).
source: For COX2 RNA, on changing from the growth condition yielding a high [NAD+] / [NADH] ratio to the growth condition yielding a low [NAD+] / [NADH] ratio, we observe a decrease in levels of NAD+ capping (from ~50% to ~20%) and an anti-correlated increase in the level of NADH capping (from ~10% to ~40%).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A comparing different growth conditions.

claim: Changing from a growth condition yielding a high [NAD+] / [NADH] ratio to a growth condition yielding a low [NAD+] / [NADH] ratio results in an anti-correlated increase in the level of NADH capping of COX2 RNA (from ~10% to ~40%).

claim: The total level of NAD+ and NADH capping of COX2 RNA remains constant (~60%) under different [NAD+] / [NADH] ratio conditions.

claim: S. cerevisiae and human mitochondrial RNAs are capped at substantially higher levels than non-mitochondrial RNAs.

evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of data in Figures 4 and 5 to prior work on non-mitochondrial RNAs.
